source.title: Grokking as a First Order Phase Transition in Two Layer Networks
source.authors: Noa Rubin; Inbar Seroussi; Z. Ringel

record.tranche_reason: The study reports delayed-generalization results on a finite synthetic teacher-student task and describes a first-order feature-learning transition; this is a conceptual test of grokking-like generalization, not a direct reproduction of the original algorithmic-task setup.
record.gate_note: The study's own finite-data results in Figures 5–6 are included. Its modular-arithmetic analysis is an equilibrium calculation, not a time-course of train/test accuracy; the modular-arithmetic experiments it mentions are cited from Gromov (2023) and are not recorded as this study's results. The linear-component plots are omitted because the text does not describe delayed learning there.
record.test_reason: The only time-course results (App. D, Figs 5–6) show delayed generalization on a synthetic non-algorithmic task: a Gaussian-input Erf teacher-student regression. The delay appears only once width is reduced from the GP-like regime (N=2800) into the feature-learning regime (N=700). This is a new setting with a result on V3, not a reproduction of the original recipe. The main-text results are equilibrium phase-transition analyses with no time axis.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. More precisely, the authors map grokking onto a first-order phase transition: a mixed Gaussian-mixture feature-learning phase in which some neurons specialize to the teacher. They derive this analytically in the equivalent-kernel limit for a cubic teacher and for modular addition. They show finite-data experiments where this transition comes with delayed test-loss improvement. They conjecture that first-order phase transitions are a potential mechanism of grokking.
record.recipe_differences: The finite-data result uses an Erf teacher-student regression setup, Langevin dynamics, and a width sweep; it is not the original small algorithmic dataset training recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The finite-data behavior varies with network width: the reported sharp test-loss drop occurs at N = 700, and the study describes continued cubic-component learning in narrower networks.

fits_no_version.finding: First-order phase transition in the weight posterior along the teacher direction, driven by width (Fig 4) or by noise σ² (Fig 2a,b). New minima at w·w*≈±1 appear, giving a mixed GMFL-I phase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking corresponds to a first-order phase transition in the hidden-weight distribution, with a mixed phase of specialized and unspecialized neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: At equilibrium, the cubic-component learning shows a sharp transition as a function of σ² near 0.18 (Fig 2c), at n=3000, far below the NNGP requirement of about 0.5e6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature-learning phase transitions reduce sample complexity relative to the GP limit.

fits_no_version.finding: In the modular-addition theory, the test-RMSE proxy a goes from −1 to −0.7 across the GMFL-I interval (σ²≈0.227 to 0.175, P=401). This is a 30% discrepancy reduction as a function of noise, not of time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking as a function of a control parameter (noise or sample size) at equilibrium.

record.problems: The reported delayed-generalization evidence is on a synthetic teacher-student regression task and uses loss/component projections rather than accuracy. Figure 5 does not give textually stated numerical loss values or a width-specific description for N = 1400 and N = 2800. The authors note that the main analytical treatment uses the equivalent-kernel limit, which washes out the train/test generalization phenomenon; the time-dependent evidence is confined to the supplementary finite-data experiment.
record.rows_left_out: Cited modular-arithmetic experimental results from Gromov (2023) were excluded because they are not this study's results. Figure 6's linear-component projections were omitted because the text does not describe them as delayed-generalization findings.

untested.parts: Images, text and molecules; initialization scale or weight norm as the switch (width is the knob here); accuracy rather than loss.
No time-course on an algorithmic dataset. The modular-addition part is an equilibrium calculation, and the delay-versus-training-set-size relation is not tested.
Varma et al. is cited only. Weight decay is part of the Bayesian prior, not tested as a cause; there is no ungrokking or critical-size test.
No comparison of learned algorithms across runs.
Langevin training is used throughout, but optimizer or numerical artifacts are not examined as a cause of the delay.

missing.what: The σ² dependence of the delayed-generalization effect (small σ² gives EK, no gap; large σ² fails both train and test)
missing.locator: Supplementary Material D, text before Fig 4

record.verdict_notes: The record's second limits_scope label (component projections are not accuracy) states a measurement caveat, not a scope limit; it is replaced. Width-driven onset of the delay, moving out of the GP/lazy regime, is analogous to V3's lazy-to-rich switch, but it is not initialization scale or weight norm. The modular-arithmetic time-course results are Gromov (2023)'s and are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The finite-data experiment uses a nonlinear teacher-student regression task, not a small algorithmic dataset, and does not report training/test accuracy or a sweep over training-set size.

The paper analyzes feature-learning phases, but does not track a generalizing circuit forming gradually, removal of memorizing components, or continuous progress measures anticipating an accuracy jump.

Tests delayed generalization on a synthetic non-algorithmic teacher-student task, with network width as the varied parameter. It does not test images, text, molecules, initialization scale, or weight norm as switches.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
The study does not test an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking. Its use of weight decay in the modeling setup is not a test of those claims.
The study does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
The study does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts cause the delay.

relationships.condition: Finite-data Erf teacher-student regression (n=600, d=150), Langevin training, narrowest width N=700 (and N=1400 for component projections)
relationships.reason: Test loss plateaus then drops sharply at N=700 (r2). Test-side cubic-component learning continues after train-side learning saturates (r7, r9). The delay appears only after width is lowered out of the GP-like regime. All values are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Test loss plateaued before dropping sharply at width 700, and test-side cubic learning continued after training-side saturation once width left the Gaussian-process-like regime.

relationships.condition: Choice of GPR noise σ² in the finite-data experiment
relationships.reason: The authors say small σ² approaches the EK limit, where the delay is washed out, and large σ² fails on both train and test. The delayed-generalization signal therefore depends on choosing σ². This rests on the App. D text, not on any row.
relationships.display_finding: Small noise variance washed out the delay near the equivalent-kernel limit, while large noise variance caused both training and test failure.
